extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology/economics; readers of social theory
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt of sociological theory (Veblen) describing norms and motives governing dress, fashion, and the leisure class — explaining how conspicuous waste, leisure, and reputability shape apparel and social institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous waste as dominant norm of dress
rubrics_metrics.description: The great and dominant norm of dress is the broad principle of conspicuous waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress should display wasteful expenditure; wastefulness functions as the primary social standard shaping apparel. This norm controls matters of dress and constrains acceptable innovations (e.g., garments permitted for only a brief term increase wastefulness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous leisure as subsidiary norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsidiary to conspicuous waste is the principle of conspicuous leisure: dress signals that the wearer does not and cannot engage in productive labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress construction includes contrivances that show exemption from productive work (e.g., impracticable bonnet, corset, high heels). Such signals mark social status by evidencing inability or exemption from manual labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Up-to-dateness / novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Dress must at the same time be up to date — fashions must be current and constantly change from season to season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty can be understood as a corollary of conspicuous waste (short lifespans of garments increase waste), but novelty also functions as a creative/aesthetic motive: innovations seek forms more acceptable to aesthetic sense while conforming to expensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation constrained by expensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Each successive innovation in fashion must not only be more beautiful (or less offensive) but must also meet the accepted standard of expensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic improvements are limited by the norm of conspicuous waste — new styles must display enough cost to be reputable; otherwise they fail as status signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonism between expensiveness and artistic apparel
rubrics_metrics.description: The norm of conspicuous waste is incompatible with the requirement that dress should be beautiful or becoming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wastefulness is intrinsically ugly because it implies futility; thus fashion innovations simulate usefulness to avoid outright ugliness, producing transient contrivances that soon provoke aesthetic rejection and further change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion's transient 'beauty' due to reputability and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: New styles are felt beautiful while novel and reputable, but this alleged beauty is transient and spurious and fails the test of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of new fashions stems partly from relief of novelty and partly from reputability shaping taste; persistent aesthetic judgment later rejects the transient fashion as grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate of fashion change correlates with offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The more rapidly styles succeed and displace one another, the more offensive they are to sound taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faster turnover implies more intrinsically odious styles; increasing wealth/mobility intensifies conspicuous waste and accelerates fashion changes, producing more grotesque styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable national/popular costumes vs. fluctuating modern fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain relatively stable, localized national costumes are often judged more becoming and artistic than the fluctuating modern civilized styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable costumes arise among poorer, more homogeneous, immobile populations where conspicuous waste asserts less imperatively and pecuniary emulation emphasizes conspicuous leisure rather than consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of reputability requires wasteful expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of reputability requires that dress should show wasteful expenditure; reputability shapes taste and enforces display of expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputability can make aesthetically dubious features acceptable so long as they signal status; when novelty or reputability passes, fashions are rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation of usefulness to avoid aesthetic condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashionable details strive to avoid condemnation by showing some ostensible purpose, yet the requirement of conspicuous waste makes such purpose largely a transparent pretense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because wastefulness is offensive, fashionable contrivances often feign utility (make-believe usefulness) to temper disgust; when the make-believe deteriorates into obvious futility, the style is rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-specific markers: garments that imply incapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain items (high heel, skirt, corset, impracticable bonnet) are evidences that the wearer does not and cannot habitually engage in useful work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such garments are deliberately uncomfortable or disabling to display leisure and dependent economic status; their persistence depends on class structure and industrial development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's dress as vicarious consumption and reputability
rubrics_metrics.description: Woman's apparel more insistently testifies to exemption from productive employment; women's dress is contrived to put in evidence their household's ability to pay — the woman's sphere is to display the household's good name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The social system delegates the function of honorific expenditure and conspicuous leisure to women; historically women were required to display unproductiveness and sometimes to disable themselves for this purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male restraint in displaying incapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wasteful expenditure and show of abstention from effort cannot, when carried to obvious discomfort or disability, be displayed by men without implying inferiority rather than superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men's dress must not indicate incapacity for productive labor to the same extent as women's; otherwise the signal would defeat its honorific purpose by suggesting weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priestly and servant vestments as vicarious consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Priestly vestments and servants' livery show evidence of servile status and vicarious consumption — ornate, inconvenient garments indicating that repute accrues to an absent master, not the wearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priestly attire is designed to be expensive and comfortless to show vicarious consumption; the priest/servant functions are analogous in economic symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of class markers during periods of snobbery/transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Features like the corset persist in use where they serve as evidence of honorific leisure; they remain common in societies or strata still in transition from lower to upper pecuniary grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The corset survives among later accessions to wealth and in countries with lower industrial structure; persistence indicates snobbery — an intermediate period of social ascent where plebeian canons of taste linger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of status signaling as affluent class grows
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sufficiently large wealthy class develops and its members acquire skill in interpreting subtle signs, advertising methods refine toward subtler, more delicate signals of expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loud or obvious dress becomes offensive to taste; honor is sought from the cultivated sense of one's own class, prompting subtler contrivances that require trained observers to detect—leading to amelioration of dress for wider society over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/institutional conservatism: institutions as habits of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions are habitual methods of life and ways of thinking inherited from the past; they are conservative factors (social/psychological inertia) and adapt only slowly to changed circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change in institutions requires changes in habitual views; classes sheltered from environmental pressures (e.g., the wealthy leisure class) adapt more tardily, retarding social transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic (pecuniary) pressure as primary engine of institutional readjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Readjustment of institutions in modern industrial communities is chiefly driven by economic forces — pecuniary exigencies translate environmental pressure into motives for changing habits of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals who must change their means of livelihood are most incentivized to reconstruct received schemes of life; thus economic pressure compels changes in habits and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective adaptation and conservation in social evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Social evolution proceeds by a process of selective adaptation and conservation of favorable variations (including selection between ethnic types or adaptation within types); institutions evolve by natural-selection-like processes of habits being conserved or discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions that once fit past circumstances may not fit altered conditions; social progress depends on the capacity of members to adapt, which is shaped by exposure to environmental forces and the distribution of pecuniary pressures.
